summary: Suggests an experimental protocol that lets a host send a short message to be shown to a user on another host. Hosts may experiment with it. It was replaced by RFC 1312.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to flash a short note onto a friend's screen on another computer.

questions: send a message to a user on another host
how do i send a message to a user on another host
subtitle: A lightweight way to flash short messages between computers on the Internet.

tldr.problem: Some hosts want to send short messages to users on other hosts without the overhead of TCP, similar to the Unix write command but across the network.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol defines two services: one uses TCP on port 18 and one uses UDP on port 18. A message contains a version byte, a target user name, terminal name, and the message text, all null-terminated and limited to 512 octets.
tldr.outcome: This experimental protocol never saw wide adoption; RFC 1312 replaced it. SMTP's SEND command provides a TCP-based alternative with less code overhead than full TCP would suggest.

today: RFC 1159 is Experimental. It was replaced by RFC 1312, which defines the current Message Send Protocol.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content: The Message Send Protocol (RFC 1159) solves a specific problem: some hosts run TCP/IP only part of the time, and for those hosts, the full overhead of a connection-based protocol is impractical for a simple task like flashing a short message to a user's screen. The protocol provides a lightweight alternative to deliver a short message to a specific user on a specific terminal on a given host, similar to the Unix write command but across the network.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer cannot run full network protocols all the time, it still wants to send quick notes to users on other computers.

sections.title: Two Service Options
sections.content:
The RFC defines two versions of the service. The TCP-based version uses TCP port 18: a client connects, sends the message, and the server sends the same data back (which the client ignores), then closes the connection. The UDP-based version uses UDP port 18 as well: the client sends a datagram, and the server echoes it back. Both approaches carry the same message format.

The message structure has four null-terminated parts: a single-octet protocol version (decimal 65, the ASCII character 'A'), the target user name, the terminal name (or empty to pick the right one automatically), and the message text itself. The entire message must be under 512 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send a message either through a fast connection (TCP) or a quick packet (UDP). Both ways put your message in four parts: the version, who to send to, which screen, and what to say.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Notes
sections.content: The RFC advises implementations to strip escape sequences before delivering messages to actual terminals, to prevent hostile input from causing problems. Checksums are always used in both TCP and UDP versions. The RFC explicitly notes that security issues are not addressed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers should be careful about strange characters in messages so they do not break the terminal, and the protocol includes safety checks.
